svg.title: One piece of evidence or two? Prerequisite course
svg.text: One piece of evidence or two? — Prerequisite course

Circularity between the Gene Ontology and pathway databases in enrichment analysis. M2 Bioinformatics, Programming unit, 2026–2027. Every claim points to a reference from biblio.md, in clickable blue brackets; “Brief”
brackets point to the project brief.
What you will be able to do after this course
1. Read a GO annotation line and say where it comes from: resource, evidence code, reference.
2. Explain the four mechanisms by which GO and pathway databases depend on each other.
3. Compute by hand an enrichment test, a Benjamini-Hochberg correction and a Jaccard index.
4. Show on an example how double counting inflates the agreement between GO and pathways.
5. Evaluate an LLM judge against simple baselines and write a defensible pre-registration.
Structure. The course follows the seven parts of the project; each part opens with a dark banner acting as a title page,
A lesson. It asks a question in blue, explains it in prose on the left, works it through an example or a figure on the right,
then closes with three boxes: the key idea (blue), the trap (red) and what it means for you (grey).
Diagram colours. Green = established in the literature; dashed orange = to verify on your own files; dashed purple =
choice to freeze in the pre-registration; red = risk; blue = information. The full legend is at the end.
Course map: which parts answer which project questions

The project asks three questions [Brief §2]. Q1 measures the share of GO annotations derived from a pathway database; Q2 measures the effect of this circularity on enrichment agreement; Q3 tests whether an LLM detects evidence counted twice.
Arrows show which notions you need before tackling each question.
What share of GO BP annotations derives from
Does GO / pathway agreement drop without
Can an LLM judge whether two pieces of
the pre-registration frames Q2 and Q3
The Gene Ontology: a graph of terms and annotations that carry their provenance

Before talking about circularity, you need to know what a GO annotation is, how it propagates through the ontology and what its accompanying fields say. These fields (evidence code, reference, assigned_by, With/From) are
exactly the ones you will use to rebuild provenance in step 1.
GO is a directed acyclic graph: annotating a term means annotating all its ancestors
Why does a gene annotated to “double-strand break repair” also count for “DNA repair”?
Sources: GO 2023 · GO 2026 · Rhee 2008 · Gaudet & Dessimoz 2017 · Brief §3
Three vocabularies. GO describes gene products along three aspects: molecular function,
cellular component and biological process [Rhee 2008]. The project is restricted to biological
processes (BP) in humans [Brief §1]. The GO knowledgebase comprises the ontology itself, the
annotations and, more recently, GO-CAM models [GO 2023].
A graph, not a tree. Terms are linked by typed relations (is_a, part_of, regulates), and a term may
have several parents [GO 2023]. In the example, “DNA repair” is both a DNA damage response
and a DNA metabolic process: two paths lead up to the root.
Propagation. A gene annotated to a specific term also takes part in every more general process
that contains it. The annotation is therefore propagated to ancestors, along the is_a and part_of
relations used in the brief [Brief Tab. 1]. Not all relations are transitive in the same way, and this
is one of the classic misreadings of GO [Gaudet & Dessimoz 2017].
What the example shows. Three genes and three direct annotations are enough to make six
terms “annotated”. A gene list enriched for “DNA repair” will be almost mechanically enriched for
its parents: this is redundancy within GO, which the project keeps apart from circularity between
A moving target. The ontology and its annotations are revised continuously [GO 2026]. Versions
must therefore be frozen and recorded at the start [Brief §3].
Simplified extract, check it in your go-basic. Dashed arrows stand for several intermediate terms. G1, G2 and G3 are
annotated directly to the orange terms; the black badge gives “direct annotations / genes counted after propagation”.
A direct annotation holds for every ancestor of the term: counting
a term’s genes assumes you have propagated.
Propagating along every relation, regulates included, or forgetting
The pre-registration must say whether you propagate, before or
after the C0–C3 classification, and how NOT qualifiers are
An annotation is a sourced statement: who made it, on what evidence, from what
Which GAF fields tell you where an annotation comes from?
Sources: GO 2023 · Good 2021 · Gaudet 2011 · Brief §1, Tab. 1, annex B
One annotation, one line. A GO annotation is an evidence-backed statement that a gene product
has a given functional characteristic [GO 2023]. In GAF files each annotation is one line of
tab-separated columns, which the project reads for the BP aspect [Brief Tab. 1].
Four fields carry provenance. The evidence code says which type of argument supports the
annotation; the reference (DB:Reference) says which document; With/From says which other
object the inference relies on; assigned_by says which resource produced the line [Brief §1]. The
step-1 provenance graph is built from these four columns.
Reading line A. It is produced by Reactome, with code TAS and a Reactome reference.
Reactome supplies the consortium with a file of such annotations, all TAS [GO report 2026]. The
GO annotation and the Reactome pathway are then one and the same curation, seen twice.
Reading line B. It carries code IBA and, in With/From, a PANTHER tree node: it was inferred by
phylogenetic propagation within a PANTHER family [Gaudet 2011]. The consortium figure shows
the same logic in the interface: each annotation displays its contributor, code, PANTHER family
What does not show. An annotation derived from a GO-CAM model converted from Reactome
does not necessarily carry “Reactome” in assigned_by [Good 2021]. The assigned_by field alone
Lines built for this lesson, identifiers elided: do not look them up in GOA. Highlighted rows are the four fields that carry
Original figure — [GO 2023], Fig. 1, CC BY licence, reproduced unmodified. (a) terms and relations; (b)
annotations with contributor, evidence code, PANTHER family and reference; (c) GO-CAM model.
An annotation’s provenance is read from four columns: evidence
Classifying on assigned_by alone: annotations from
The provenance table (annex B) keeps these fields for each
The evidence code says how an annotation was obtained, not whether it is true
What does a code such as TAS, IBA or IEA tell us about dependency between two resources?
Sources: Rhee 2008 · Gaudet & Dessimoz 2017 · Škunca 2012 · Gaudet 2011 · Tomczak 2018 · GO report 2026
A type of argument. Each annotation carries an evidence code: experimental, phylogenetic,
electronic, author statement, and so on [Brief §1]. Misreading these codes is among the most
Not a reliability score. Electronic annotations are often deemed unreliable, but their reliability
has improved markedly and now rivals that of curator annotations based on evidence other than
published experiments; over 98% of annotations are made without direct curation [Škunca 2012].
Excluding a code “because it is weak” would be a different debate from the project’s.
A provenance clue. For the project, the code is above all a clue about dependency. TAS flags a
statement traced to a source, and the file supplied by Reactome is entirely TAS [GO report 2026].
IBA flags an inference on a PANTHER tree, which also underlies PANTHER pathways
A coverage bias. Annotations concentrate on few genes: 58% of human annotations concern 16%
of genes [Tomczak 2018]. These heavily studied genes recur in many terms and pathways,
creating overlaps without any derivation between resources.
says which type of argument supports the annotation
Statement traced to a source, such
The black badge gives the dependency category this kind of code makes plausible in the project; only the pre-registered rule
decides. Code list not exhaustive: start from the codes present in your GAF.
Figures from [Tomczak 2018]: 58% of annotations concern 16% of human genes.
The evidence code classifies the type of argument; for the project
it is a dependency clue, to be confirmed by the other fields.
Reading IEA as “false” and EXP as “true”. The code does not
measure quality [Škunca 2012], and an EXP annotation can
share its publication with a pathway (C3).
Q1 proportions are to be reported overall and by evidence code, by
Pathway databases: four ways to describe a process

Reactome, PANTHER and PathBank describe chains of reactions and group the genes involved; GO-CAM links GO annotations into causal models. For enrichment, all these structures are flattened into gene sets. KEGG is
Reactome, PANTHER, PathBank and GO-CAM differ in object and in construction
What does each database hold, and what remains of its structure once it becomes a gene set?
Sources: Milacic 2024 · Thomas 2022 · Wishart 2024 · Thomas 2019 · GO 2026 · Khatri 2012 · Brief §3
Reactome. Reactome describes normal and disease processes as an ordered network of
molecular transformations, manually curated in a single data model [Milacic 2024]. Its pathways
are organised in a hierarchy, and the resource explicitly discusses its interoperability with GO
PANTHER. PANTHER reconstructs phylogenetic trees of protein families and annotates them
with function gain and loss events [Thomas 2022]. The same families underlie PANTHER
pathways and the PANTHER GO-slim [Brief §1]: remember this, it grounds category C2.
PathBank. PathBank 2.0 holds 6,951 canonical pathways and 605,359 pathways in total, with a
strong focus on drug metabolism and mechanism [Wishart 2024]. Many of them are near-identical
variants: the brief requires filtering a subset and justifying the filter [Brief Tab. 1].
GO-CAM. A GO-CAM model links several GO annotations through causal relations to describe a
system [Thomas 2019]. It is not an independent pathway database: it is a component of GO itself
[GO 2023], and part of the Reactome conversion goes through it (lesson 05).
Flattening. Classic enrichment analysis only sees gene–pathway membership; topology is used
only by a more recent generation of methods [Khatri 2012]. The project works on gene sets.
manually curated, in a single data model; aims at the
Phylogenetic trees of protein families, annotated with
function gain and loss events; enrichment tools.
Canonical pathways up from 1,720 to 6,951, and
605,359 pathways in total; strong focus on drug
GO molecular activities linked by causal relations; over
For enrichment, a pathway becomes a gene set
Reaction order, complexes and hierarchy disappear: enrichment only sees membership. You must decide whether a gene also
belongs to superpathways (propagation through the Reactome hierarchy).
A pathway and a GO term both become gene sets; the question is
whether those sets were built independently.
Treating GO-CAM as a source external to GO: it is GO itself, and
some of its models come from Reactome [Good 2021].
Versions frozen at the start, with date, number and checksum;
PathBank filter justified in the pre-registration [Brief §3].
When resources feed each other: the mechanisms of circularity

The theoretical core of the project. Four documented links tie GO to pathway databases; the literature presents them as consistency assets. The project draws the opposite consequence: agreement between two linked
resources is not an independent confirmation.
Four documented mechanisms make GO depend on pathway databases
Through which routes does the same information end up in both a GO term and a pathway?
Sources: GO report 2026 · Good 2021 · Gaudet 2011 · Thomas 2022 · Gillis 2013 · Milacic 2024
(a) Reactome writes into GO. Reactome supplies the GO consortium with an annotation file of
about 100,000 to 108,500 associations depending on the count, mostly human, all with code TAS
(release 96) [GO report 2026]. A GO BP annotation from this file and the gene’s membership of
the matching Reactome pathway are one curation: this is direct derivation, C1.
(b) Pathways2GO. The Pathways2GO tool converts the entire set of normal human Reactome
pathways into GO-CAM models, from which standard GO annotations are derived [Good 2021].
The figure shows it reaction by reaction. These annotations may not carry “Reactome” in
assigned_by: you must trace back to the GO-CAM model to detect them. This is C1 too.
(c) A shared basis, PANTHER families. Phylogenetic annotations are inferred on PANTHER
family trees with the PAINT tool: a function observed experimentally in a few members is
assigned to their common ancestor then propagated to descendants [Gaudet 2011]. The same
families underlie PANTHER pathways [Thomas 2022]. Neither resource copies the other, but they
(d) The same papers. Distinct curated resources often rely on the same publications. The
precedent is known for protein interactions: many entries come from the papers used for GO
[Gillis 2013]. A GO annotation and a pathway citing the same PMID fall under C3.
An asset turned bias. These links are presented as consistency and cross quality-control assets
[Good 2021] [Milacic 2024]. Their effect on users who read two enrichments as two pieces of
evidence has not been quantified recently [Brief §1].
Original figure — [Good 2021], Fig. 3, CC BY licence, reproduced unmodified. Two Reactome reactions (A, B) converted, via BioPAX,
into GO-CAM activity units (C, D): same entities, same locations, same causal link.
Original figure — [Gaudet 2011], Fig. 1, CC BY-NC licence, reproduced unmodified. PAINT: experimental annotations (green) are
lifted to the common ancestor (orange box), then propagated to all its descendants (blue). These propagated annotations carry code
papers read by curators of both worlds
Orange: into GO annotations. Blue: into pathway gene sets.
“GO and Reactome agree: two pieces of evidence”
If both sets share their origin, the agreement is partly mechanical.
Three structures (TAS file, GO-CAM, PANTHER families) and one
practice (citing the same papers) let one piece of evidence feed
Assuming these mechanisms instead of observing them: the brief
requires verifying them on the file versions used [Brief §4.1].
This is Q1: what share of human GO BP annotations falls under
each mechanism, and in which BP branches [Brief §2].
The C0–C3 typology turns the mechanisms into rules that can be applied automatically
How do you decide, line by line, whether a pair of evidence is independent, and what if several rules apply?
Sources: Brief Tab. 2, §5 · article draft Methods and Discussion · Good 2021
Four categories. The brief proposes an indicative typology: C0 independent, C1 direct derivation,
C2 shared basis, C3 shared reference [Brief Tab. 2]. Each category matches one mechanism
Rules, not intuitions. A category is usable only if a rule computes it from file fields (assigned_by,
evidence code, With/From, references, GO-CAM model, PANTHER family). These rules are the
main analytical degree of freedom of the study [Brief §5]: they must therefore be frozen before
Order matters. Categories overlap. A TAS annotation supplied by Reactome also cites
publications, so it can fall under both C1 and C3 [draft, Discussion]. If C1 is tested first it is
classed C1; in the reverse order it inflates C3. The flowchart applies the most direct derivation
first, but this choice must be written down and justified.
Blind spots. Annotations derived from Reactome-converted GO-CAMs do not necessarily carry
“Reactome” in assigned_by [Good 2021]. A rule based on assigned_by alone will wrongly class
part of C1 as C0. Plan an “undetermined” category rather than forcing doubtful cases.
A pair = one GO BP annotation + the same gene’s membership of a pathway
Is the annotation produced by the database or from it?
assigned_by = Reactome, or converted GO-CAM model
Do they rest on the same structure?
IBA whose With/From is a node of the pathway’s PANTHER family
Do they cite at least one common publication?
Independent: distinct resources, references and derivations
Pairs built for this lesson. The order of questions is a proposal: you must freeze it.
A pair’s category is the output of an ordered rule over file fields;
changing the order changes the proportions.
Tuning the rules after seeing the proportions or the enrichments:
this is exactly the freedom the pre-registration must close
The rule_applied column of the provenance table keeps the rule
that decided each line [Brief annex B]; the category also serves
as ground truth for the LLM judge (lesson 13).
The precedent: curated resources share their papers, and heavily annotated genes dominate the signals
What is already known about confounds between GO and other resources?
The closest precedent. Gillis and Pavlidis showed that many entries of protein interaction
databases come from the same papers as GO annotations; 66% of the assessed GO groups show
this confound [Gillis 2013]. The diagram on the right redraws this mechanism: one observation,
Why this is not the project already. That work concerns protein interactions, not pathways, and
dates from 2013. GO / pathway double counting in enrichment has not, to our knowledge, been
GO moves. Annotations are stable in the short term (3% of genes change nearest neighbour
between monthly editions), but 20% of genes change functional identity within two years
[Gillis 2013]. Enrichment results change with the GO version [Tomczak 2018].
Multifunctional genes. A gene’s degree of multifunctionality alone predicts its function
remarkably well, with no information on its partners [Gillis 2011]. These heavily annotated genes
often appear in results and produce non-specific, fragile enrichments [Ballouz 2017]. GO /
pathway agreement can therefore come from a few genes present everywhere, without any
two agreeing “pieces of evidence”… from a single observation
Diagram redrawn from the finding of [Gillis 2013]; the project transposes it to pathways (C3).
of assessed GO groups show this
of genes are no longer most similar
Two curated resources are independent only if their sources are;
shared papers and multifunctional genes are two confounds
Attributing all residual agreement to circularity: multifunctionality
also produces overlaps [Ballouz 2017], hence the null model
The null model draws random lists matched on size and
annotation degree [Brief §4.2]; this is the direct answer to that
Enrichment analysis: a simple test, choices that change everything

The project replays over-representation analyses (ORA) on about twenty gene lists. You need to understand the test, what the background universe does, why correct for multiple testing, and where redundancy and
Over-representation compares what is observed with what chance would give within a chosen universe
When is a GO term or a pathway said to be “enriched” in a gene list?
Sources: Khatri 2012 · Reimand 2019 · Wijesooriya 2022 · Klopfenstein 2018 · Brief §4.2
The question. Does a gene list from an experiment contain more genes from a given set than
chance predicts? Pathway analysis reduces a list’s complexity and increases its explanatory
power; its methods fall into three generations: over-representation, functional class scoring and
The test. We draw n genes (the list) from a universe of N genes, K of which belong to set T. If
the list were random, the number k of T genes it contains would follow a hypergeometric
distribution. The p-value is the probability of seeing at least k. In the example 2 genes are
expected and 8 observed: P ≈ 5 × 10⁻⁴. The brief cites this test as a possible choice, to be
The universe decides. N must contain the genes that could have entered the list, for example the
measured genes. Taking the whole genome artificially inflates significance, as the second box
shows. In a survey of 186 articles, 95% of ORA analyses did not use an appropriate background
Tools. The reference protocol describes three steps: define the list, determine enriched sets,
visualise and interpret [Reimand 2019]. GOATOOLS, a Python library, runs over- and
under-representation tests on GO and can sit behind your own interfaces [Klopfenstein 2018]
P(X ≥ k) = Σ C(K, i) · C(N − K, n − i) / C(N, n) (i = k … min(K, n))
Same 8 genes, same term: changing the universe divides the p-value by about ten billion. Values computed for this lesson.
Original figure — [Khatri 2012], Fig. 1, CC BY licence, reproduced unmodified. The three generations of methods: over-representation
(ORA), functional class scoring (FCS) and pathway topology (PT). The project uses the first.
Enrichment is a departure from expectation under random draws
within universe N: without a well-defined universe, the p-value
Using the whole genome as the universe for a list drawn from a
few thousand measured genes: the most frequent error in the
Test, universe, thresholds and tool (with version) must be
pre-registered and identical for GO and pathways; otherwise
Testing thousands of terms requires controlling the proportion of false positives
Why is a p-value of 0.03 not enough when testing every GO BP term?
Sources: Reimand 2019 · Wijesooriya 2022 · Klopfenstein 2018 · Gable 2022 · Brief §4.2
The problem. GO has over 47,000 terms [Klopfenstein 2018]. At a 0.05 threshold, testing
thousands of terms without correction mechanically yields dozens of chance “hits”. In the survey
by Wijesooriya et al., 43% of analyses applied no correction [Wijesooriya 2022].
Benjamini-Hochberg. Sort the m p-values, compare the i-th one with the threshold i/m · α, and
keep every rank up to the largest i that passes. This controls the expected proportion of false
positives among the results kept (FDR), which is less strict than Bonferroni, which controls the
risk of even one false positive. The table shows the effect: four terms kept versus one.
Gene-set size. Very large sets are uninformative and very small ones unstable; the reference
protocol discusses filtering them [Reimand 2019]. Term size also affects result specificity
depending on the annotation system [Gable 2022]. The brief asks for a minimum and maximum
Removal changes the number of tests. Removing C1 annotations empties some terms, which
fall below the minimum size or vanish: m changes between conditions. You must decide in
advance whether the same set of tested terms is kept across the three conditions.
m = 6 terms tested, α = 0.05. Benjamini-Hochberg keeps ranks 1 to 4 (highlighted), including rank 3, which fails on its own;
Bonferroni (threshold 0.05/6 = 0.0083) keeps only one. Values built for this lesson.
Original figure — [Wijesooriya 2022], Fig. 2, CC BY licence, reproduced unmodified. Survey of published
enrichment analyses: background rarely specified (G), FDR correction missing in a large share of analyses
With thousands of tests, control the false discovery rate (FDR);
the correction and size bounds are part of the protocol, not
Comparing conditions (all / no C1 / no C1–C3) where the number
of tested terms differs without saying so: the same term’s
q-value changes for that reason alone.
The enrichment table keeps p_value and q_value for each list ×
Redundancy and instability: results that repeat themselves and change with versions
Why does a list of enrichment results contain so many near-identical terms, and why does it depend on the version?
Sources: Strielkov 2025 · Stoney 2018 · Tomczak 2018 · Gable 2022 · Gillis 2013
Within GO. The hierarchy yields highly redundant lists of enriched terms, which makes them hard
to prioritise. evoGO down-weights a gene on a term when that gene already supports a more
significant descendant; on synthetic data, the number of enriched terms drops by about 30% while
Between pathways. Consolidated databases contain many overlapping pathways. A set cover
on ConsensusPathDB keeps 100% of genes with 74% less redundancy [Stoney 2018]. Overlap is
measured with the Jaccard index (intersection over union) or with an asymmetric overlap index,
Versions. On 104 disease signatures, results obtained with early and recent GO versions agree
poorly [Tomczak 2018]. The function attributed to a gene drifts too [Gillis 2013]. A measured
agreement only makes sense for a frozen combination of versions.
Comparing is not testing independence. Gable et al. compare eleven annotation systems on
nearly 2,000 real datasets; established, hierarchical systems give the best enrichments
[Gable 2022]. Their framework compares systems with one another but does not ask whether
they are independent: that is the project’s own angle.
Original figure — [Tomczak 2018], Fig. 2, CC BY licence, reproduced unmodified. Human GO annotations from 2004 to 2015: their
number soars and concentrates on already well-characterised genes.
Original figure — [Gable 2022], Fig. 1, CC BY-NC licence, reproduced unmodified. Evaluation design: 3,651 queries from STRING
users, 1,959 after redundancy filtering, replayed on each annotation system.
Original figure — [Stoney 2018], Fig. 1, CC BY licence, reproduced unmodified.
Set cover: first pick the set covering the most elements, then complete.
resources are two different problems; the project measures the
Confusing GO redundancy with circularity: your effect must be
The Jaccard index on driver genes is one of the proposed
agreement definitions [Brief §4.2]; propagation to ancestors, or
Double counting: when GO / pathway agreement is a data leak

Showing a GO enrichment next to a pathway enrichment, then reading their agreement as confirmation, assumes both are independent. This part shows on a worked example how circularity manufactures agreement, and
GO / pathway agreement can be manufactured by circularity: the worked example
What remains of the agreement between a GO term and a pathway once the annotations derived from it are removed?
Sources: Brief §4.2, Tab. 2 · Good 2021 · GO report 2026 · Gaudet 2011 · Ballouz 2017 · draft, Discussion
The scenario. A GO term T and a Reactome pathway P are both enriched in a list. It is tempting
to conclude that two independent resources confirm the same process. Yet three of T’s
annotations come from Reactome, through the TAS file [GO report 2026] or a converted GO-CAM
model [Good 2021], and a fourth from a PANTHER tree [Gaudet 2011].
Three conditions. The brief requires redoing the GO enrichment with all annotations, without C1,
then without C1 to C3, and comparing each time with the pathway enrichment [Brief §4.2]. In the
example, the Jaccard index of driver genes falls from 0.83 to 0.33 then 0.17: most of the
agreement came from one curation counted twice.
Define agreement beforehand. Several definitions are possible: proportion of significant
pathways linked to a significant GO term sharing a minimum fraction of driver genes, rank
correlation, Jaccard on driver genes [Brief §4.2]. One must be designated as the primary measure,
Convergence or circularity? Agreement that survives removing C1 may reflect real biological
convergence, or C2–C3 circularity that was not removed [draft, Discussion]. The null model,
made of random lists matched on size and annotation degree, says what level of agreement is
expected without any biological signal, including the effect of multifunctional genes
Studied list: A to F (plus other genes outside T and P). Driver genes of pathway P in the list: {A, B, C, D, E}.
Jaccard of T and P driver genes
Without C1, T keeps {D, E, F}: Jaccard with {A … E} = |{D, E}| / |{A … F}| = 2/6. Without C1–C3, T keeps {E, F}: 1/6.
Constructed example; the purple band shows where matched random lists would fall.
If part of the GO annotations copies the pathway, their
agreement is partly an artefact: removing C1, then C1–C3,
Removing annotations can make T non-significant: the measure
must be defined for a term that disappears too, or the most
circular cases drop out of the analysis.
This is Q2. Lists must come from experiments independent of
The unit is the gene list
Testing the effect of removal: a paired comparison, list by list
How can you conclude that agreement really drops, with only about twenty lists?
Pairing. Each list is measured twice, before and after removing circular annotations. Lists differ a
lot from one another, but what matters is the difference within each list. The statistical unit is
therefore the list, and the test must be paired [Brief §4.4].
The Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Compute the difference d for each list, rank the |d| from
smallest to largest, then sum the ranks of negative differences (W−). If removal had no effect,
each sign would be as likely as the other. Here only one list out of six increases, and it has the
smallest difference: W− = 1, p = 0.031. The test does not assume normally distributed differences,
which suits a small number of lists.
A p-value is not enough. The brief asks for an effect size [Brief §4.4]: here the median
difference, 0.165, says by how much agreement drops. An alternative is a mixed-effects model
with the list as a random effect, which also uses resources and conditions.
Set the direction beforehand. A one-sided test (“agreement drops”) is legitimate only if
announced before the data. This is what separates a prediction from an after-the-fact explanation
Under H0 the 2⁶ = 64 sign patterns are equally likely; 2 give W− ≤ 1.
Agreement before / after removing C1, per list
Values built for this lesson; L4 (red) is the only list whose agreement increases.
Compare each list with itself: the paired Wilcoxon test, plus an
effect size, on the “gene list” unit.
Treating terms as independent units: thousands of terms from the
same list are not replicates and inflate significance.
Suggested hypotheses: H2a drop after removing C1, H2b larger
drop without C1–C3, H2c residual agreement above the null model
Can an LLM see that a piece of evidence is counted twice?

Large language models can name the function of gene sets and can check their claims against curated databases. No work consulted asks them to judge the independence of two pieces of evidence from their metadata.
This part gives what is known, the protocol and how to evaluate the judge.
LLMs know gene function; judging the provenance of evidence is a different task
What is known about LLM abilities on gene function, and how do you query them without giving the answer away?
Sources: Hu 2025 · Wang 2025 · Yang 2026 · Gu 2024 · Brief §4.3, annex A
Naming a function. On curated GO gene sets, GPT-4 proposes a name close to the curated one in
73% of cases, and gives zero confidence to 87% of random sets; other models are falsely
confident on those sets [Hu 2025]. Stated confidence can thus be informative, but it depends on
Checking itself. GeneAgent confronts its own claims with expert databases through their APIs;
on 1,106 gene sets it is more accurate than GPT-4 [Wang 2025]. It is the closest work to Q3, but
the question differs: GeneAgent checks a function, the project asks whether two pieces of
Knowing or reasoning. On knowledge published after their training, LLMs do markedly worse
than on established knowledge [Yang 2026]. A judge that recognises a Reactome–GO dependency
may have read it in documentation during training: the article draft asks you to discuss this
Judge biases. LLMs used as judges have known biases: position, verbosity, preference for their
own outputs [Gu 2024]. The order of the two pieces of evidence is therefore randomised at each
query, and each pair is queried three times [Brief §4.3].
The anti-leak rule. The prompt contains only raw metadata, as found in the files; never the
expected category nor any hint at how the ground truth was built [Brief §4.3]. Otherwise you
measure the model’s ability to read back the answer.
GAF, Reactome, PANTHER, PathBank: raw metadata of both pieces of evidence
no expected category, no hint about how ground truth was built
fields filled by code; A/B order randomised at each query
exact model id, date and raw response archived
non-conforming answers and majority vote: pre-registered rules
Protocol from the brief, annex A and §4.3; flowchart redrawn for this lesson.
Original figure — [Wang 2025], Fig. 1, CC BY licence, reproduced unmodified. GeneAgent: generation,
self-verification against databases through their APIs, modification, then summary.
The judge receives raw metadata and nothing else; the rest of the
protocol makes its answers comparable and reproducible.
Letting the ground truth leak into the prompt, through a computed
field, a file name or a fixed presentation order.
Queries are run in session with the teacher; the annex A prompt is
used in English, unmodified [Brief §4.3, annex A].
Evaluating the judge: per category, against simple baselines, with enough pairs
How do you know whether the LLM judges better than a trivial rule, and which dependency types it misses?
What is measured. The brief asks for accuracy, sensitivity and specificity per category,
calibration of stated confidence and stability across the three queries [Brief §4.3]. With
“dependent” as the positive class, sensitivity is the share of C1–C3 pairs recognised as
dependent, and specificity the share of C0 pairs recognised as independent.
The accuracy trap. The sample is stratified: three categories out of four are dependent. A judge
that always answers “dependent” therefore reaches 0.75 accuracy, more than the example LLM
(0.70), without understanding anything. Balanced accuracy and per-category results put the judges
Simple baselines. The LLM is compared with a constant answer and a rule based on the
assigned_by field alone [Brief §4.3]. In the example, the rule catches all C1 but no C2 or C3; the
LLM recovers part of C2 and C3. This is exactly the question “which dependency types does it
Comparing two judges on the same pairs. McNemar’s test uses only pairs where the two
judges disagree [Brief §4.4]. With 11 pairs versus 3, p = 0.057: the difference is inconclusive. The
number of pairs must therefore be fixed in advance, accounting for this limited power.
Calibration. A confidence of 0.9 should be right nine times out of ten. For GPT-4, higher
confidence goes with answers closer to the curated name [Hu 2025]; you must check whether
this holds for your different task.
“Positive” = dependent (C1–C3). Stratified sample built for this lesson: 10 pairs per category.
McNemar: LLM versus assigned_by rule, on the same 40 pairs
LLM does better on 8 more pairs, but
40 pairs are not enough to conclude at
A judge is evaluated per category and against trivial baselines; on
a stratified sample, accuracy alone rewards the constant answer.
Claiming the LLM is better from a gap of a few pairs: with 40
pairs, McNemar is still non-significant at 11 versus 3.
Suggested hypotheses: H3a, the LLM beats the best baseline;
H3b, its sensitivity is lower for C2 and C3 than for C1
Pre-registration: freezing choices before seeing results
Every previous part left choices open: C0–C3 rules, universe, correction, agreement measure, judge protocol. Pre-registration freezes them, publicly and dated, before the analysis.
Pre-registering separates what was planned from what was discovered along the way
Why deposit the protocol before the analysis, and how do you do it when the data already exist?
TO DO AT THE START OF WEEK 2
Sources: Nosek 2018 · van den Akker 2021 · Brief §5
Predicting or explaining afterwards. Science advances by generating hypotheses from existing
observations and testing them on new ones. Confusing the two reduces credibility, and hindsight
bias makes the confusion hard to avoid. Defining the questions and the analysis plan before seeing
Why here. The project piles up legitimate choices: classification rules, universe, correction,
thresholds, propagation, agreement measure. Each combination is a different study; the example
already counts 64. The C0–C3 rules are the main analytical degree of freedom [Brief §5].
Data that already exist. GO, Reactome, PANTHER and the gene lists are published: this is
secondary data analysis. A dedicated pre-registration template exists for this case, and practical
strategies allow pre-registering when data pre-exist [van den Akker 2021] [Nosek 2018]. You
must declare what you have already seen of the data during the pilot.
Deviate, but say so. A deviation is allowed if it is dated, justified and reported in the paper;
unplanned analyses are welcome if labelled exploratory [Brief §5]. Q1 is descriptive; Q2 and Q3
2⁶ = 64 possible analyses on the same data
With only two options per choice, there are already 64 versions of the study. If the one that “works” is picked afterwards,
the reported p-value no longer means anything. Example built from the choices listed in Brief §4.2.

The course in fifteen sentences, vocabulary, self-check and sources
Reread this page before writing the pre-registration: each sentence sums up a lesson and points to the decision it requires.
01. GO is a graph: a direct annotation holds for all ancestors, provided you propagate along the right relations.
02. An annotation’s provenance is read from four fields: evidence code, reference, With/From, assigned_by.
03. The evidence code gives the type of argument, not its quality; TAS and IBA are dependency clues.
04. Pathways and GO terms become gene sets; only how they were built matters.
05. Reactome’s TAS file, Pathways2GO, PANTHER families and shared papers tie GO to pathways.
06. The C0–C3 typology is an ordered rule over file fields, to freeze before analysis.
07. Shared papers and multifunctional genes already create demonstrated confounds.
08. Enrichment is a departure from expectation within a given universe: the universe makes the p-value.
09. With thousands of tests, control the FDR, and conditions must test the same terms.
10. Redundancy within GO and version drift are distinct from circularity.
11. Removing C1 then C1–C3 measures the share of GO / pathway agreement manufactured by circularity.
12. The effect is tested list by list, paired, with an effect size.
13. The LLM judge receives only raw metadata, in random order.
14. The judge is evaluated per category and against trivial baselines, with enough pairs.
15. Pre-registration freezes the choices and makes deviations visible.
assigned_by — GAF column naming the resource that produced the annotation.
BP — Biological Process, the GO aspect studied in the project.
C0–C3 — relationship categories between a GO annotation and a pathway: independent, direct derivation, shared basis,
Evidence code — type of argument supporting an annotation (EXP, IDA, IBA, IEA, TAS…).
Agreement — pre-defined measure of agreement between GO and pathway results.
Double counting — reading as two pieces of evidence what comes from one source.
FDR — expected proportion of false positives among results kept.
GAF — tab-separated GO annotation file format, one annotation per line.
GO-CAM — model linking GO annotations through causal relations.
Driver genes — genes of the list that belong to the enriched set.
IBA — annotation inferred on a PANTHER family tree (PAINT).
Jaccard — size of the intersection divided by that of the union of two sets.
McNemar — test comparing two judges on the same pairs through discordant pairs.
Null model — matched random lists giving the agreement expected without signal.
ORA — over-representation analysis, e.g. by hypergeometric test.
PAINT — phylogenetic curation tool producing IBA annotations.
Pathways2GO — tool converting Reactome pathways into GO-CAM models.
Propagation — carrying an annotation over to all ancestors of the term.
Pre-registration — dated deposit of the protocol before analysis.
TAS — Traceable Author Statement: statement traced to a source, code of Reactome annotations.
Universe — set of genes that could have appeared in the list.
Wilcoxon — signed-rank test comparing two paired measures.
With/From — GAF column naming the object the inference relies on.
1. A gene is annotated to “DNA repair” with the NOT qualifier. Should it count for “DNA metabolic process” after propagation? Why?
2. An IEA annotation has assigned_by = UniProt and comes from a GO-CAM model converted from Reactome. What would an assigned_by-only rule say, and what is the right category?
3. Redo the lesson 08 test with k = 5: does the p-value fall below 0.05 in a 1,000-gene universe?
4. In lesson 11, what would the no-C1 Jaccard be if gene F were annotated to T only by IBA?
5. Why does a judge that always answers “dependent” beat the LLM on accuracy in lesson 14, and which metric fixes this?
6. During the pilot you ran an enrichment on a selected list. What must the pre-registration say about it?
